item-13|ds: These two 18th-century British pianos — the 1796 Broadwood baby grand and the 1781 Ganer square piano — were developed for a postgraduate project. They were recorded inside the anechoic chamber at ISVR, University of Southampton, with contributions from professor, musician, and composer David Owen Norris, as a collaboration between the Institute of Sound and Vibration Research and the university's Music Department. The Broadwood has three pedal variations (no pedals, una corda, sustain), and the Ganer square piano has eight variations of dampers and buff stops.

item-16|ds: A while ago, at an antique store, I stumbled upon this old crystal mic from the 1950s. Remarkably it still works great. I planned to make a few instruments with it, starting with an old-fashioned choir sound — recording myself singing a few notes (poorly, I might add) and arranging them into this instrument. It's silly but fun, and sounds kind of cool in a lo-fi way.
item-56|ds: To my ears, this is a little gem of sound design of the kind I love to find. The Cogeco Amphitheatre is a well-known venue in Trois-Rivières, Quebec, for its shows and events; with a bit of work, some of its characteristic sounds — set manipulation, or wind slipping through a door — capture its atmosphere. All the sounds used here were captured on the stage and its surroundings.
item-58|ds: A Persian harp. I've listened to and tried many samples — many have great sounds and effects, but I decided to make just one. I hope you enjoy it! Greetings from Mexico!
item-65|ds: The jaw harp, also called the juice harp, mouth harp, or Jew's harp, is a fun one-note instrument. By striking a metal tongue between two metal extrusions framing either side, and placing the frame against your teeth, you generate a tone amplified by your open mouth. Changing the position of your lips and tongue further shapes the note. Simple, but a lot of fun — hopefully you enjoy it as much as I do!
item-66|ds: Merry Christmas and Happy Holidays, everyone! What better way to celebrate the season than with a free, simple instrument sampled from authentic sleigh bells, with a twist — one of the bells is fake! Hope everyone's holidays are full of cheer and you have fun with this silly little instrument.
item-101|ds: Over the last two months I went through a phase of modular synthesis. Not having the budget for my own Eurorack hardware, I asked around for software alternatives and was pointed toward VCV Rack, a great hardware emulator that lets you record the patches you make as audio or video. I designed my own patch using two main oscillators, a texture synthesizer for granular synthesis, and some built-in effects. When I sampled it, the texture synthesizer — which was monophonic in the original patch — became polyphonic, a nice added bonus I hadn't expected.
item-132|ds: All sorts of discoveries are made in an old basement. Here you'll find a variety of sounds from clock gongs rubbed with a bow. The middle and lower octaves are generally softer and more pleasant to play, while the higher octaves (marked in red) lean more into sound-design territory and are best used one note at a time.
item-109|ds: Hello everyone, I'm delighted with Pianobook — I've found so many of the coolest tools here and keep adding to my collection! Thanks to everyone who helped build this project, and to everyone who shares their sample libraries. I wanted to contribute too, so here's my library of a Crafter electroacoustic guitar (MD70-12EQ/TBK)! It's originally a 12-string guitar, but since I'm still fairly new to playing, I kept only six strings in the classical formation (EADGBE). I only meant to borrow this guitar from my colleague Julia to record it and give it back, but playing it fascinated me so much, and it sounded so beautiful, that I decided to buy it.
item-123|ds: One of these discoveries made while walking near a vent. Use the sounds here as you like — as WAV files or through the plugin, as-is or modified — just don't resell them. This sound bank is free; feel free to share it. It comes with basic features and effects so you can experiment yourself.
item-125|ds: I've been loving my Moog Sound Studio 3, so I made a few patches to share with everyone. Since not everyone has a DFAM, I sampled these patches so you can still have fun with them even without the hardware. If you make anything cool with this, feel free to share it — I'd love to see what you create!

item-165|ds: What started as me browsing Amazon one night turned into this rather unique sample library. The Gjallarhorn — also known as a Viking warhorn or sounding horn — is a unique instrument made from an ox horn. It can really only produce one pitch consistently and is fairly difficult to play, relying on the vibration of your lips being amplified by the shape of the horn. It's unique and rather silly, but hopefully you get as much enjoyment from it as I did making it.
item-185|ds: While in college, I took some classes that let me build my own circuits. Recently, while working on side projects, I had time to reflect on some of those old experiments. I cleaned a few of the circuits up and built simple cases for them using old tins I'd saved around the house. These are some of those experiments — I recorded a few notes (poorly, I might add) and arranged them into this instrument.
item-187|ds: A hurdy-gurdy. I've listened to and tried many samples — many have great sounds and effects, but I decided to make one with a wider range. I hope you enjoy it! Greetings from Mexico!
item-213|ds: Thank you for downloading my sample library, "Lofi Dreams." This is my third sample library uploaded to Pianobook. I apologize for any issues — I'm continuously trying to improve. I noticed one problem: when the release is set to 0, there's a clicking sound at the end when you release the key. I'm working on fixing it and will update the library once it's resolved.
item-296|ds: My partner noticed my fascination with sampling and knew I loved ringing sounds, so she bought me a singing bowl for my birthday. It has a wonderful ring, and I thought it would make a good instrument. I sampled it in my bathroom (the quietest room in the flat!) with a Tascam DR-40x in XY mode, using a soft felt beater.
item-301|ds: I'd been wanting to program velocity layers and round robins together for a while, so I took the opportunity to practice with a small lap harp labelled "Cymbalon" on the box — a trapezoid-shaped sound box with a circular sound hole in the centre and 15 strings, fairly commonly found on auction sites. I chose a string close to 'C', tuned it, and sampled it with a Tascam DR-40x in XY mode. The usable range runs from C0 to C6.
item-322|ds: This is the sound of a city fountain, captured through the Ether device by Soma Laboratory. It's an instrument that's definitely nothing traditional, but still very musical.
item-345|ds: This is a small part of a much larger project involving a visual-feedback generative installation: generative analog music gear feeding into CRTVs with cameras, with the resulting animations altered by the sounds created.

item-366|ds: This hybrid percussion library is the result of a graduation project. It combines orchestral percussion elements with processed industrial sounds, creating a distinctive hybrid palette. Designed primarily for action cues — trailers, combat sequences, and high-intensity moments in film, TV, and video games — though its range of timbres and textures allows for creative use in other genres too. Percussionists: Juan Rafael Moreno Echeverry, Juan David Agudelo, Ricardo Morán Marín, Santiago Gómez Ríos, Juan David Posada Jaramillo, and Juan Pablo Mesa García.
item-49|ds: African xylophone. I've always been drawn to African instruments; in this case, I made a simple modification to the sounds of a xylophone a friend had put away at his house, aiming for a clearer sound without effects. I've tried many samples with great sounds and effects, but decided to make one with a wider range instead. Low and high tones spanning four octaves (Bb–F). I hope you enjoy it!
item-72|ds: For a long time I've been very fond of brass sounds; this time I recorded simple sounds and arranged them for a clear tone, using a bass trombone. The sounds aren't from my own instrument — they came from a wind-instrument sample database.
item-238|ds: A wind instrument (duduk) built from natural recorded sounds.
item-15|ds: This library was made from my antique 1930s Wurlitzer upright, a piano I've had since I was 6 years old when I started taking lessons. It includes a pizzicato preset (plucking the strings with my fingers, producing a harp-like sound).
item-230|ds: Uses 3 round robins — 3 discrete samples per note per velocity layer. On the lowest sampled note, a fret noise was included.
